transcript:
MEETING HEADER
Date: 2028-04-26
Start: 09:34 AM PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Ethan Keller (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Marcus Li (CTO - Auriga Decisioning), Jenna Park (Lead ML Eng), Omar Ruiz (SRE), Leila Hassan (PM)

SUMMARY:
Auriga is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private for real-time decisioning at the edge. Primary focus is p95 latency for streaming scoring and throughput under burst (token/sec and concurrent streams). They want concrete token/sec benchmarks, fallback behavior, and a clear cost/latency tradeoff.

TOPICS COVERED:
- p95 targets and how to spec them per route
- streaming vs complete generation latency differences
- concurrency and burst sizing (steady state vs 5-10s spikes)
- cache/warm start effects on KV cache and prefix caching
- private deployment constraints (VPC, KMS, SOC2)
- test artifacts: benchmark spreadsheet and representative prompts

ACTION ITEMS (in call and follow-up): see metadata action_items field

TRANSCRIPT:
[00:00] Ethan Keller: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, we have about 50 minutes, let's run through the latency/throughput goals and then get into specific benchmark asks. Marcus, do you want to kick off with your goals?
[00:18] Marcus Li: Yeah sure, thanks. So quick context: we do real-time decisioning for ad-serving and fraud mitigation, things need to be very snappy. Our current p95 for a typical scoring call is around 200ms but that's without heavy prompt context, as soon as we stream long contexts it jumps. Goal is 200-300ms p95 for a 128 token streaming finish, and for longer generation paths like 1k tokens we'd accept higher but want predictable tail.
[00:45] Jenna Park: to add, about 60% of our calls are streaming token-by-token for the decision output, the others are batched inference for offline scoring. The streaming ones are the most critical — we need consistent p95 under load spikes up to 250 concurrent streams.
[01:05] Priya Shah: ok that's super helpful. When you say streaming 128 tokens at 200-300ms p95, do you mean end-to-end from HTTP ingress to first partial token or to completion?
[01:15] Marcus Li: good call out — we mean to first meaningful token / time-to-first-byte, not full generation. Full completion for 128 tokens can be relaxed.
[01:26] Ethan Keller: cool, so time-to-first-token p95 target ~250ms for streaming. We'll talk about what that looks like on hosted vs dedicated vs private. Quick qual question — do you have any constraints on data residency or encryption that would push you to private?
[01:40] Leila Hassan: We have PCI-adjacent data flows, so audit logs and KMS integration are must-haves. We prefer dedicated if it meets latency, but private if we need full VPC isolation.
[01:52] Omar Ruiz: also SSO and RBAC for operators, and long-term audit log retention, like 7 years for specific flows.
[02:03] Priya Shah: totally reasonable. From Redwood's side, hosts: hosted gives fastest onboarding but shared tenancy; dedicated gives pinned GPU pools with predictable throughput and lower noisy neighbor variance; private gives full VPC + KMS. All three can meet SOC2 and SSO; private has the deepest network isolation.
[02:22] Jenna Park: can you talk about the model variants and quantization impact on latency? Our stack uses a medium-sized open model now, thinking of moving to quantized 4bit variants.
[02:34] Priya Shah: absolutely. Quantization typically lowers memory footprint and increases concurrency by letting more k-v cache fit in VRAM, but for some models it can add a slight p95 tail due to dequant/requant overhead — we can show per-model profiles. For streaming TTFB it's mostly kernel latency and attention window; for 4-bit often net positive for throughput.
[02:55] Marcus Li: ok. Second qual: our traffic is bursty, typical baseline 80 concurrent streams, but during peak campaigns we see 400-600 concurrent for short 30-90s bursts. How does Redwood handle that?
[03:11] Ethan Keller: good scenario — Dedicated allows reserved nodes and autoscale with burst capacity; the key is how you define SLOs. We recommend a steady-state commit for baseline, with burst policies that either use on-demand capacity or fallback to a lower-cost/latency tier. Also autoscaling warm-up can be tuned to your burst profile.
[03:29] Priya Shah: also prefix caching and KV cache re-use reduce cold-starts. If identical prefixes are hot, per-request latency can be much lower — we can instrument the cache-hit rate in our benchmark sheet.
[03:41] Omar Ruiz: what's the overhead for cold cache vs warm? like if we scale from 80 to 500 quickly, do you have numbers?
[03:49] Priya Shah: rough numbers — cold cold-start for a new worker and model weights: tens of seconds for a full host spin-up in bare VMs, but in Dedicated we keep a hot pool and can serve in sub-second for token TTFB; the dominant cost is KV cache warm — first few requests might be 2-5x slower. We'll capture exact numbers in the microbench.
[04:10] Ethan Keller: to be explicit, for streaming TTFB target ~250ms p95 we need a combination of hot pool, kernel-optimized model, and steady KV reuse. We'll run a microbench to show token/sec and time-to-first-token under bursts.
[04:23] Jenna Park: what about multiplexing? We have limited GPU budget but want to host many small models per tenant. How does concurrency packing affect p95?
[04:33] Priya Shah: multiplexing is great for utilization but increases variance; continuous batching and smart routing helps. For a strict p95 SLO you might want dedicated slices or guaranteed pools per critical route. We can show utilization vs tail plots.
[04:45] Marcus Li: awesome — on benchmarks, what artifacts do you need from us?
[04:49] Ethan Keller: the spreadsheet — traffic histogram (RPS over day), representative prompts (top 20), SLO per route (TTFB p95, completion p95), and any resource constraints. We'll also ask for a sample VPC network diagram if you think private is likely.
[05:03] Leila Hassan: we'll provide that.
[05:07] Priya Shah: practical test plan I propose: 1) microbench for token/sec: single model, varying concurrency 10, 50, 200, 500 for 128-token streaming; 2) end-to-end latency trace with realistic prefix distributions; 3) burst profile test for 90s windows to see autoscale & cold effects. We'll attach scripts and the benchmark spreadsheet.
[05:28] Ethan Keller: timing-wise we can deliver initial microbench results within a week. That'll include CSVs and a summary sheet.
[05:34] Marcus Li: great. A few more technical Qs — how do you route across regions if we have multi-region decision points? We need geo-fallbacks and consistent latency across US/EU.
[05:47] Priya Shah: Redwood supports policy-based routing — you can prefer region-local model endpoints and have an automated fallback to a secondary region. For consistent latencies we recommend warm pools in both regions and prefer local model variants. We can show failover latency numbers.
[06:02] Omar Ruiz: and the observability — do you provide token-level latency breakdowns? e.g., kernel time vs network vs batching delay?
[06:09] Ethan Keller: yes, Redwood Console exposes token-level breakdowns, per-route dashboards, and traces you can link to your APM. We'll provide sample screenshots.
[06:20] Jenna Park: security: KMS integration, do you support customer-managed keys for private?
[06:25] Priya Shah: yes, private supports KMS/HSM integrations, plus audit logs exported to your SIEM. Hosted supports envelope encryption with Redwood KMS or customer keys for enterprise plans.
[06:36] Marcus Li: if we start with Dedicated, how hard is it to move later to Private? What's the friction?
[06:42] Ethan Keller: migration path is straightforward — Dedicated uses the same control plane and APIs, so you can pin configs and eventually migrate to private control plane. Network setup and cert provisioning are the main tasks. We'll share a migration checklist.
[06:56] Leila Hassan: cost sensitivity — can you ballpark token cost delta hosted vs dedicated vs private?
[07:02] Ethan Keller: ballpark: hosted per-token can be higher due to multi-tenant overhead but lower ops. Dedicated has lower per-token when committed capacity is used efficiently. Private has additional infra and ops fees; we'll send detailed tiers.
[07:15] Marcus Li: ok. On fallback policies — if primary model is saturated, can the system fall back to a smaller quantized model automatically?
[07:23] Priya Shah: yes, we have policy-driven fallbacks — you can specify model variants and routing priority. We can also do dynamic routing by latency budget. For example, if p95 exceeds 300ms, route to a smaller model for degraded-quality but faster response.
[07:36] Omar Ruiz: do you have A/B style rollouts? we want canary traffic split for new model versions.
[07:41] Ethan Keller: yes, rollouts and canaries are first-class in Console.
[07:45] Jenna Park: let's talk benchmarks — what would your microbench report look like?
[07:49] Priya Shah: CSV with columns: concurrency, stream_ttfb_p50/p95, tokens_per_sec, token_latency_breakdown (kernel/batching/network), cache_hit_rate. We'll include plots.
[08:02] Marcus Li: can you also measure the end-to-end p95 from our SDK side? We want to include our networking overhead.
[08:08] Priya Shah: yes we'll run both internal (agent-side) and e2e (customer network) runs. We'll need your test endpoint or a VPN access for private.
[08:19] Ethan Keller: ok let's annotate specific SLO rows: Route A (real-time short streaming): TTFB p95 <= 300ms, concurrency burst up to 600 for 90s, baseline 80. Route B (batch scoring): completion p95 <= 2s for 1k tokens.
[08:34] Leila Hassan: that matches our internal thinking. One more ask — can Redwood run a token/sec stress test that simulates heterogeneous prompts? Not just uniform length.
[08:44] Priya Shah: yes, we can parameterize prompt distributions. Please provide top-20 prompts and their frequency.
[08:50] Marcus Li: we'll do that.
[08:53] Ethan Keller: great. On timeline: we'll run microbench and share by 2028-05-03, pricing + SLO draft by 2028-05-01, and then propose a POC kickoff the week of 2028-05-08.
[09:06] Marcus Li: sounds good. Let's call out the key risk — KV cache warm-up during very short bursts may cause p95 slips, so we need to see warm-pool sizing.
[09:17] Priya Shah: yep noted — we'll include warm-pool sizing recommendations.
[09:21] Omar Ruiz: logging — can you export raw per-token logs for a 30-day window? We need to analyze anomalies.
[09:28] Ethan Keller: yes for Dedicated and Private we can export logs to your S3 or SIEM, hosted has options for aggregated traces.
[09:37] Jenna Park: ok wrapping up, any blockers on Redwood side to get started?
[09:41] Priya Shah: none, just access to the prompt set and traffic histograms, and confirmation whether you want hosted/dedicated/ private POC.
[09:50] Leila Hassan: we'll aim for Dedicated POC first.
[09:53] Ethan Keller: perfect. I'll send the benchmark plan and a link to the benchmark repo and sheet. Priya will own the microbench run.
[09:59] Marcus Li: thanks Ethan, Priya. One last item — can you show a sample routing policy that does geo-fallback + model fallback? A doc would be perfect.
[10:08] Priya Shah: yes we'll include a sample policy snippet in the follow-up and notes.
[10:12] Ethan Keller: ok, thank you all. We'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule the POC kickoff.
[10:18] Marcus Li: thanks, bye.

MEETING RECAP (auto):
- Primary goal: validate that Dedicated meets streaming TTFB p95 ~250-300ms with bursts up to 600 concurrent streams for short windows.
- Redwood to run microbench and provide token/sec, TTFB p95, cold vs warm numbers by 2028-05-03.
- Customer to provide prompts, traffic histogram and confirm POC scope.
- Next meeting: POC kickoff week of 2028-05-08.

REFERENCES SHARED:
- Benchmark spreadsheet (link sent in chat)
- Redwood SOC2 and private deployment checklist (to be sent)
- Example routing policy snippet (to be attached)

END OF TRANSCRIPT
